titleStmt.title: Estimation and analysis of communication service time in a real-time wireless industrial network

analytic.title: Estimation and analysis of communication service time in a real-time wireless industrial network

div.p: Wireless communication systems for industrial applications should cope with the demanding performance figures of real-time wired networks, providing high reliability and satisfying tight timeliness constraints. The implementation of a scheduling framework may represent a relevant method to deploy real-time behavior in distributed measurement, process control and supervision networks. A schedulability analysis, based on task parameters, determines if the network will be able to provide the guarantees required by the specified application. Nonetheless, this strategy and the related error recovery mechanism are often implemented at a high level protocol layer, without carefully considering the behavior of physical/data-link layers of the network. An effective characterization of the service time for packet delivery, as seen by the data link-layer, is instead required for a fine tuning of the scheduling algorithms.

We analyzed the case of an IEEE 802.11g based network, where a central scheduler manages the traffic. We derived a model for the transmission times, in particular accounting for retransmissions due to channel impairment and interference. An improved model for the service time is then proposed, based on a cross-layer analysis. This allows to reshape the statistical knowledge of the metric, hence improving the network performance and admission test outcomes. The provided casestudy enables the reader to understand the effectiveness of the proposed method, which provide a reliable soft real-time data acquisition system.

div.head: I. Introduction
div.p: Communication networks employed in the industrial environment for measurement, process control and supervision purposes, are required to comply with demanding performance figures. As a consequence, the most common choice is to exploit the robustness and reliability of wired networks (such as Profinet, Ethernet/IP, etc) based on the Real-Time Ethernet (RTE) profile [1].

The adoption of wireless networks may bring several interesting advantages. These include the connection of mobile components, significant reduction of cabling costs and the simplification in network deployment or maintenance [2], [3]. The downside is that communication over wireless channels is intrinsically error-prone and non-deterministic [4], so that such benefits come with a set of relevant challenges. Key requirements of field-level industrial communications are timeliness, reliability and determinism. Conversely, a wireless channel may continuously change due to several phenomena, e.g., moving obstacles in the transmission path, multi-path propagation, interference by other communication devices, etc. When wireless networks are adopted, which is today increasingly the case, an effective method to provide similar real-time (RT) performance figures is the adoption of a RT scheduling framework.

In this specific framework, network operations follow a centralized approach, where a controller node polls the attached field devices (e.g. sensors and actuators) to gather their data through scheduling policies [5], [6]. Each communication with the field is hence a periodic task, that must be completed within a specified deadline.

In the scientific literature the problem of implementing scheduling on a wireless system has already been considered in the past [7], [8]. Unfortunately, this has often been tackled at a high protocol level, modeling lower layers simply by a given probability of wrong transmission [9]. Hence two main actors, i.e. the scheduler and the link-layer protocol, play a crucial role in this framework, yet in a non-cooperative way, giving rise to possibly serious loss of performance, which may hamper a more widespread adoption af wireless transducers in RT measurement and automation.

Considerable improvements could be achieved if the RT scheduler is made aware of the features provided by the underlying protocol structure, in terms of both the expected transmission time and retransmission scheme, in a typical crosslayer approach, involving the physical (PHY) and medium access control (MAC) layer [10].

In this paper we provide a model for link-layer packet delivery time in a typical IEEE 802.11g based network, which for the implementation of wireless extensions is the most likely candidate in a wired RT Ethernet environment [11]. We specifically consider the MAC and PHY layers of the standard and, stemming from the defined channel access algorithm and backoff procedure, we derive a simple and effective model for the service time, i.e. the time needed to complete a packet transmission at the link-layer.

We show that service time may be affected by a high degree of randomness, being conditioned on the probability of transmission error. A suitable statistical approximation of the evaluated service time is provided, and a relevant confidence level proposed. An effective lower value for the maximum expected service time is finally obtained, which can be included in the admission test performed by the scheduler, thus optimizing the behavior of the scheduling algorithm.

div.head: II. Problem Statement
div.p: A central node implementing an RT scheduler manages a set of field nodes through a high level protocol layer based on a polling scheme, in which the controller polls the attached nodes for data collection, thus realizing a RT packet pair.

The transmission of periodic RT packets m i is modeled as a task characterized by a period T i . A maximum transmission time C i and a deadline D i , are also specified. This means that when data are available in a specific field node, they must be delivered to the network manager within the assigned deadline D i , while the actual transmission time, i.e., the RT packet service time, is upper bounded by C i , with C i < D i .

Since data packets are periodic, a table, listing all RT packets m i , i = {1, . . . , Q} and their relevant parameters, is held by the RT scheduler so that it can trigger the transmission of the correct RT packet. To construct this table, the scheduler initially (offline) performs an admission procedure on the whole set of RT packets m i , i = {1, . . . , Q} in order to verify their actual schedulability, i.e., if a particular choice for the packet transmission sequence exists to meet all the existing deadlines. The test is affected by several factors, such as transmission scheme (i.e.modulation) and channel model, though is mainly influenced by the packet deadlines and transmission times. A successful admission test allows network operations to start.

It is worth noting that in an RT perspective, several approaches could be pursued for data management. For example one might expect a hard RT behavior, where there is no possibility for a deadline to be missed. One can also pursue a soft RT approach, where deadlines can be occasionally missed, with an accepted a-priori probability. Although such design choices do influence the outcome of admission tests, the main parameter is the "execution time" of tasks which, in the case of communication networks translates into the service time of an RT packet.

These considerations justify the need for a reliable and effective model for the packet transmission time C i , together with methods for the estimation of model parameters, so that the scheduling algorithm can be adequately optimized. The main contribution of this paper is the development and validation of a model based on cross-layer analysis, which represents a significant departure from most existing works on the subject. Indeed, analyses carried out in the literature [6], [9] focus on the high protocol layer characterization, rather than addressing the influence of the lower layers, that in turn are regarded as a "black box" exhibiting a given probability of error. Since packet errors are likely to occur in a wireless link, the controller typically adopts an Automatic Retransmission Query (ARQ) approach, performing an immediate new attempt to gather data from the field [6]. However, at the link-layer protocol level a high number of retransmission attempts have often already occurred, in which random backoff delays have been introduced as a typical mechanism for enhancing network reliability. As a matter of fact, the scheduler at the application layer is typically unaware of what happened at the linklayer, in a non-cooperative attempt to obtain a successful data exchange with the field node. Failure to realize the interplay between the two layers thus results in actual performance being poorer than predicted. The proposed cross-layer approach allows to ultimately improve the network performance, since a better model for service time enables an increase in the number of RT packets that the controller is able to serve.

div.head: III. Network Configuration
div.p: We restrict our analysis to the specific case of IEEE 802.11 networks [12]. In particular, we will refer to the Extended Rate PHY (ERP-OFDM) physical layer and the basic DCF channel access procedure, that is, to the legacy popular IEEE 802.11g nodes. The choice is justified by the performance this standard is able to provide, which is, at least theoretically comparable with those of wired industrial networks. Moreover the industrial communication scientific community showed a remarkable interest in this specific protocol [13], [14]. Therefore, let us consider a wireless network including N devices, as shown in Fig. 1, each one hosting one or more RT packets to be periodically delivered within specified deadlines. Due to the periodicity of the scheme, we can associate a RT packet to a process identifier having specific properties (deadline, period, etc). The central station, which implements the RT scheduler, manages the RT traffic by means of a suitable scheduling algorithm. Specifically, we consider Earlier Deadline First (EDF), which has been proven to be able to guarantee adequate performance, particularly in the presence of tight timing requirements [15].
The parameter C i is composed by the sum of the time intervals necessary both to poll a node by sending a data request and to receive the actual data from the node, that is
div.formula: C i = T Poll + T Data,i i = 1, . . . , Q(1)
div.p: Eq. ( 1) is the overall transmission time for a packet, from the scheduler point of view. It is worth observing that, in this context preemption is not allowed, no matter what is the scheduling algorithm, since it is not possible to interrupt a RT transaction on the network, yet technically feasible.

In order to ensure an acceptable reliability the system shall implement some error recovery method. A typical choice is the adoption of a common ARQ scheme directly managed by the scheduler at the application protocol level. Accordingly, after a "data request" is triggered towards the slave, the scheduler waits for the subsequent data packet, which should arrive within a time-out interval. If this is not the case, the transaction is rescheduled with the same absolute deadline. The timeout time T T O,i is chosen as:
div.formula: C i < T T O,i < D i , i = 1, . . . , Q(2)
div.p: A direct consequence is that, since also packet retransmissions have to be accounted for, the scheduler shall ensure that all the transmission attempts are completed within the packet deadline D i . However, the scheduler is typically not aware of another type of retransmissions that may occur at the lower protocol levels, here called MAC-retransmissions.

Without loss of generality for industrial applications, we can assume that the application layer is directly connected to the MAC layer of the IEEE 802.11g stack, whose operations are regulated by the DCF procedure. This means that each unicast transmission at link-layer shall be acknowledged. Specifically, the link-layer behavior can be roughly summarized as follows: after a packet has been received from the application layer, the channel is sensed by the station for a fixed time (distributed interframe space (DIFS)) and the transmission could start if it is found free. After the request reception at the field node, a short interframe space (SIFS) is waited prior the acknowledgment packet, signaling a correct reception, is sent. In the meanwhile a countdown timer was activated by the transmitter waiting for the reception of the ACK. If an answer is not received within the ACK timeout time T ACK T O , the transmission is assumed as failed. This starts the retransmission procedure, and before each new attempt the source station waits for a backoff time, that is, a random time interval drawn from a uniform distribution, introduced in order to statistically avoid an immediate transmission failure due to a "bad" channel behavior, whose duration is exponentially increasing with the number of transmission attempts.
Indeed the duration of the random backoff time is calculated as:
div.formula: t BO (n) = T S LOT • U [0, CW(n)](3)
div.p: where T S LOT represents the slot time, a physical layer dependent parameter; U [0, CW(n)] is a uniformly distributed integer random variable ranging from 0 to CW(n), the contention window size at transmission attempt n. The window size is updated following the equation:

A successful transmission restores the value of the contention window to its minimum value CW min . The effect of the DCF procedure has thus to be represented in the Eq. ( 1), in order to obtain a more accurate evaluation of C i .

div.head: IV. Model for the Transmission Times C i
div.p: In the scheduling framework introduced in Section II the traffic in the wireless network is managed in such a way that an implicit collision avoidance mechanism is introduced, since only one task can be activated by the scheduler in a specific instant. Anyway, interference could arise from other coexistent wireless systems; moreover a non-negligible probability of error may be experienced due to the intrinsic unreliability of the wireless channel [16], [17]. Hence, the service time C i for an exchange of RT packets may present a high degree of randomness, as it can be easily argued considering that linklayer retransmissions involves the backoff times specified by Eq. (3).

div.head: A. Theoretical Characterization of the Service Time
div.p: We firstly provide an analytic evaluation of C i , based on the specifications of the IEEE 802.11g DCF layer. Since the number of MAC-retransmission executed for a correct delivery of the RT packets is clearly unknown in advance, we assume that C i takes values in the range [C min i , C max i ]. The simplest case arises when no MAC-retransmissions are needed, i.e. a transaction is completed correctly at the first attempt. In this particular case there is no randomness associated to the service time, which can be expressed as:
div.formula: C min i = T IFS + T d,req + T ACK + T d,rep(4)
div.p: where T IFS is a constant period of time resuming all the interframe spaces introduced by the IEEE 802.11g specifications, that is, the time waited before each of the two packet transmissions to sense the channel, and the short time interval waited before the acknowledgment packet. The other three terms refer to the transmission times T d,req for the data request packet, the corresponding acknowledgment T ACK and the data reply packet T d,rep , respectively. Table I provides the values for these terms. The transmission times have been calculated assuming that the scheduler requests data using packets with a 6 Byte payload, while the slave replies with a packet whose payload is 24 Bytes. The chosen sizes are small enough to emulate a typical situation found in industrial RT control networks [18]. From the values found in Table I, Eq. ( 4) yields C min i = 172 µs, which is the best-case (i.e. the minimum) for the transmission time. Nonetheless, C min i can not be used in an admission test, where a worst case scenario is expected.

As a step toward the final model let us introduce packet errors in the computation of C i . To this regard, it is worth observing that in the basic DCF procedure, the acknowledgment packets are transmitted at most at the same speed as the relative data packet, so that it is very unlikely that an acknowledgment is lost in the transmission path. For this reason, we henceforth take into account only that errors may happen only on data packets. Let us consider that j transmission are needed to correctly deliver the data request packet to the field node, whereas field node packets are correctly received at the first attempt. That is, we have a total of j-1 MAC-retransmissions. Under these hypothesis, the general expression of C ( j,1) i results as follows:
div.formula: C ( j,1) i = T IFS + T ACK + + j • T d,req + T d,rep + ( j -1) • T ACK T O + (5) +T S LOT •         j-1 s=1 U 0, 2 3+s -1        
div.p: The final expression for the service time C i is an easy extension of the last equation. Indeed, C ( j,k) i represents the service time when j transmission attempts are needed for the scheduler to request data, and k further transmission attempts are necessary to reply with the data packet. The complete expression is given by:
div.formula: C ( j,k) i = T IFS + j • T d,req + T ACK + k • T d,rep + +( j + k -2) • T ACK T O + (6) +T S LOT •         j-1 s=1 U 0, 2 3+s -1 + k-1 t=1 U 0, 2 3+t -1        
div.p: In Eq. ( 6) one can observe that deterministic terms due to the physical transmission of packets contribute to C i linearly with respect to j and k. Moreover, the random contribution to the service time is represented by the sum of j -1 and k -1 uniform integer random variables, due to the introduction of the backoff times between each transmission attempt, respectively for the controller-to-node path, and the reverse one. The upper bound for these variables increases exponentially as the number of transmission attempts increases.

The model in Eq. ( 6) has been firstly implemented in a numerical simulation. From the scheduler point of view, a first order approximation of Eq. ( 6) is given by the worst case for the service time, obtained if the maximum number of transmission attempts is consumed both at the controller and at the node, that is C (7,7) i . The analysis of the particular cases obtained letting j = k, ∀ j ∈ [1,7] in Eq. ( 6) is therefore of main interest, and shown in Fig. 2. The lower and upper lines show the minimum and the maximum theoretical values for C i , respectively. However, considering the theoretical worst case behavior for C (7,7) i likely leads to an over estimation of the service time. Consequently, claiming a higher time for a RT task to be completed, brings to a reduction of the number of periodical RT packets that can be served by the network.

div.head: B. Proposed model
div.p: We hence propose to apply known statistical methods, as those adopted for example in [19], to effectively describe and model the service time.

Indeed, Eq. ( 6) provides a full knowledge of the service time behavior. Moreover, the specific case of RT industrial traffic allows for some hypothesis to be introduced, as will be detailed later. As a result, we can consider the backoff time as the sum of independent uniform random variables, and approximate its final probability distribution, finally defining a suitable range within the service time should likely fall. This allows for a simpler description of C ( j,k) i and it may result in a significant improvement for the initial admission test of the network, actually implementing a cross-layer approach.

In the following we limit our discussion to the simpler case j = k, that is only the cases C ( j, j) i are considered, and henceforth the superscript indices will be omitted. Moreover, it is worth considering that for j < 3 the aforementioned modeling has a weak adherence with the real behavior of the system, which behaves deterministically for j = 1, and has a simple uniform description for j = 2.

As a consequence, hereinafter only cases for j ≥ 3 are specifically dealt with. Let us introduce some significant hypothesis on the specific application in mind. These communication networks are typically characterized by "non-saturated" traffic [20], [21], that is, nodes in the network may not have data to transmit at some time instant, as it is clear in the case of low-throughput periodic traffic. Moreover, limiting the analysis to j = k cases further simplify the modeling of transmission delay with respect to typical Markov-chain approaches found in the literature [22], yet providing an accurate picture of a RT industrial network. Under these hypothesis, the last line of Eq. (6) shows that C i includes the sum of at least 4 uniform random variables, which can be effectively considered as independent each other. 1 Moreover, if they were taken in pairs, they are also identically distributed, i.e. iid random variables.

The density function of the sum of two random variables is the convolution of the prior density functions, and the support of the new distribution is roughly given by the sum of the base supports. Considering the range for the uniform random variables in Eq. ( 6), for each j we have that the support of the obtained distribution is given by: Following the noticeable result stated by the Central Limit Theorem, one may recall that the sum of two iid uniform r.v. has a symmetric triangular distribution, and that their sum quickly approaches the normal distribution. In the given range the backoff time can be hence effectively modeled as a normal random time, The mean, ∀ j ≥ 3, can be calculated as:
Also, from the independence of r.v., the variance of this approximated probability distribution σ 2 (C i ) is given by the sum of the variances of the uniform backoff times.

Finally, the goal is to define an interval that has a high level of confidence, or coverage probability for the range of variation of the service time. Specifically, in an industrial real-time application, subject to scheduling, the goal is to keep the number of missed deadlines as low as possible, that is, to realize a very reliable "soft" real-time system. Therefore, following common methods of statistical analysis, as for example those adopted in [19], we introduce a coverage factor k p , such that with a very high probability the time C i is likely to be within the interval defined by this model. In the approximation of the backoff time with a normal distribution, the choice of k p = 3 assures a confidence interval of 99,73%, which seems to be a good trade off between the need of timeliness and real-time guarantees

Please consider also that from the Central Limit Theorem, the coverage factor k p for the normal distribution, given a confidence level, is higher than the k p one would obtain from the convolution of uniform distributions. Therefore considering k p = 3 provides a confidence interval even higher than the expected one. The final model in Eq. ( 8) represents a reliable approximation of the service time of a wireless link over IEEE 802.11, as seen by a link-layer perspective in a worst case approach. The values provided by this model are found in Table II. As a mean of validation of the obtained result, Eq. ( 8) has been implemented in a simple Montecarlo experiment: approximately 100.000 packets have been exchanged between the controller and a single field node using the typical parameters specified in Table I, at the maximum transmission rate allowed by IEEE 802.11g standard, 54 Mb/s. The outcomes of this experiment are shown in Fig. 2. In the figure, boxes represent the interval between the 25th and the 75th percentiles around the mean value. Whiskers highlight the interval ±3σ around the mean. Moreover, the red dots are the outliers with respect to the quoted intervals. The statistics obtained through the experiment are detailed in Table II, which clearly highlights that the difference between the theoretical maximum C i and the maximum obtained through the proposed approximation is relevant, being in some cases in the order of some milliseconds. Moreover, Table II reports also the number of outliers, i.e. how much RT packets were not delivered within the upper bound given by 3σ. Only outliers above the upper bound are significant in this case, and hence taken into account here. It is worth pointing out that, while the absolute number would change in a new execution, the obtained values have been always on the ratio 1/10000, better that the expected confidence interval chosen.

V. Remarks In this paper the case of RT industrial wireless networks has been considered, where a scheduling framework is introduced in order to enable a soft RT behavior and increase timeliness. The problem has been faced through a cross-layer approach, looking at the transmission delay from the physical/data-link layer perspective, recognizing that an effective tuning of the admission test for the scheduler would require an accurate knowledge of the packet service time at the link-layer. This would effectively avoid a relevant number of deadline misses and serve the highest possible number of RT packet flows from the field.

We hence considered the IEEE 802.11g standard, and the basic DCF medium access method. Starting from the theoretical expression for the service time, based on a critical analysis of the standard, we proposed an improved and effective model, with the purpose of optimizing and fine-tuning the scheduler, which hence becomes aware of the underlying physical layers. The model is based on the approximation of the service time probability description with a normal distribution, and the exploitation of a suitable coverage factor to obtain the very high confidence level required by the application at hand. Data have been provided, showing the effectiveness of the model. As a matter of fact, in a simulation including a hundred thousand complete packet exchange, the number of deadlines misses due to the proposed approach, with respect to the strict theoretical limit, has been in the order of some tenth, in the ratio of 1 .
